clue.text: Credit's bad? Switch to these!

indicators.note: to switch things is to swap them around, so the letters change places

blocks.note: every letter of these two words, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Friendly advice to someone whose credit rating has sunk: change how you pay.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: rearrange the letters of the first two words and you get the cards a person with bad credit is told to switch to.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone refused credit can still pay from their own bank balance using plastic that draws money directly from the account.

clue.text: Commercial retrospective repeatedly displaying nihilistic art

indicators.note: a retrospective looks backwards, so the letters are read from the end

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial on television
the same word again, since repeatedly means more than once

explanation.surface: A gallery's retrospective of advertising keeps showing art that rejects meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' looks like an art exhibition noun, which suits the surface, but it turns the short word for an advert backwards; 'repeatedly' then doubles it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dada was the early twentieth-century anti-art movement that mocked reason and convention, often described as nihilistic.

clue.text: Polish expert

blocks.note: first meaning: to rub something until it shines
second meaning: an enthusiast who knows a subject well, as in a film fan

explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes it read as a specialist in Poland; at the start of the clue it is just the verb meaning to shine.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for rubbing a surface to a shine and also a noun for a knowledgeable enthusiast.

clue.text: Ultimate success, stealth deployed by the French: I don't like it

indicators.note: troops deployed are spread out into new positions, so the letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
la is a French word for 'the'
an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: Someone sniffs at a victory won by sneaky French tactics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I don't like it' reads as a comment on the whole scene, but it is just the grunt of distaste that ends the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the final triumph after earlier setbacks is the idiom for being proved right or winning in the end.

clue.text: Got back engraved bust right away

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so its letters are smashed into a new order
sent away means removed, so one letter is taken out

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for right, and it is the letter dropped

explanation.surface: Someone recovered an engraved bust, the sculpture of a head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a carved head to go with 'engraved', but it means broken. 'Got back' is the idiom of getting back at someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To get back at someone is to take revenge on them, which is exactly what this past-tense verb describes.

clue.text: Displaying un chose, his art mimicked plumbing, primarily!

definitions.text: Displaying un chose, his art mimicked plumbing, primarily!

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives only its opening letter

blocks.clueFragment: Displaying un chose, his art mimicked plumbing
blocks.note: the initials of these seven words

explanation.surface: An artist exhibited an ordinary object, and his art looked like plumbing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: Marcel Duchamp exhibited a urinal, 'Fountain', as art. 'Un chose' is French for 'a thing', a nod to his ready-made objects.
explanation.definitionFit: The French artist became famous for presenting a manufactured urinal as a sculpture, the best-known ready-made in modern art.

clue.text: Conceited runner? Not half!

indicators.note: only half is wanted, so the second half of the word is thrown away

blocks.note: a runner can be someone who runs contraband, as in gun-runner

explanation.surface: Asked whether an athlete is big-headed, someone answers with the British 'Not half!', meaning 'very much so'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for emphatic agreement, but here it literally keeps half of an eight-letter word for a runner of goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone excessively pleased with themselves and their own qualities, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Everyman 'so robust': on the contrary, he reached age of 969!

indicators.note: the contrary is the opposite way round, so this piece is turned back to front

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself, so his name gives the first-person pronoun
so and thus both mean 'in this way'
hale means healthy and strong

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of his toughness, then is outdone by someone who lived to a record age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' looks like a retort to the boast, but it only turns round the word for robust. A setter naming himself in a clue usually means ME.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis this patriarch lives 969 years, the longest lifespan recorded in the Bible, so his name means a very old man.

clue.text: German quality of woodwinds: always wanting more

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for German
woodwind instruments sound through reeds, so their quality is being reedy

explanation.surface: A music critic describes the tone of German wind instruments as insatiable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quality of woodwinds' sounds like a review of an orchestra section, but it is a made-up noun for sounding like a reed.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed is the constant desire for more than one needs, so the noun names the state of never being satisfied.

clue.text: After Disruption, find Free Church deviation

indicators.note: something that has been disrupted is thrown into disorder, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church historian: after the Disruption of 1843, look for how the Free Church of Scotland departed from the old one.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point to real history, the 1843 split that created Scotland's Free Church, but 'Disruption' simply tells you to scramble the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A deviation is a departure from a norm, and a difference is the way two things fail to match, a close synonym.

clue.text: A little misty-eyed ... because of this?

definitions.text: A little misty-eyed ... because of this?

indicators.note: only a little of the phrase is wanted, a short stretch from inside it

blocks.note: four letters running across the hyphen

explanation.surface: Someone's eyes are watering slightly, and the clue asks whether this is the cause.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also defines the answer: a sore swelling on the eyelid can leave the eye a little watery.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed infection of an eyelash gland that can make the eye water, hence the misty look.

clue.text: Loft and hearth he renovated for spouse

indicators.note: a renovated building has been reworked inside, so these letters are rebuilt in another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man does up the attic and the fireplace for his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a home-improvement story; every letter of the first four words is reused, and 'for' simply joins them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal idiom for a husband or wife or long-term partner, the person who completes a couple.

clue.text: Dog's fine, in Ghana mobile hospital, dressing removed from wounds

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so the letters move around
a dressing covers a wound on the outside, so taking it off strips the outer letters

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
taken as written
H is the map and road-sign abbreviation for hospital
the word with its first and last letters stripped off

explanation.surface: A field report from Ghana: the dog is fine at the mobile hospital, and its wounds have had their dressings taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile hospital' reads as one thing, but 'mobile' belongs with the country before it and the hospital is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a tall long-haired sighthound breed originally from the mountains of Afghanistan, so it is an example of a dog.

clue.text: Apologies and attempts to hide a piece of underwear

indicators.note: hiding something means wrapping it out of sight, so the outer word conceals the inner

blocks.note: tries are attempts
a vest is an undershirt in British English

explanation.surface: Someone says sorry and tries to conceal an undergarment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apologies' reads as saying sorry, but here it is the sense in 'a poor apology for a meal': a shoddy imitation. In Britain a vest is worn under a shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: An apology for something can mean a feeble substitute, and a travesty is a grotesque or absurd imitation.

clue.text: At last, Danny Dyer runs a reform school, of sorts

indicators.note: at the last means at the very end, so only the final letter is kept
to re-form is to form again, so the letters are put into a new shape

blocks.note: the closing letter of the name
taken as written

explanation.surface: The actor Danny Dyer, known for tough-guy roles, finally ends up running a young offenders' school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reform school' reads as one phrase, but 'reform' is the scramble signal and 'school, of sorts' is the definition. Danny Dyer is a British actor known for EastEnders.
explanation.definitionFit: A day nursery looks after and teaches preschool children during working hours, so it is loosely a kind of school.

clue.text: Offered response when director quit (having undergone censorship)

indicators.note: whoever quits leaves, so that letter departs from the word

blocks.note: D is a standard abbreviation for director
a censored document has had passages blacked out, that is, redacted

explanation.surface: A film director walked out after the studio cut the film, and someone gave a statement about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket makes the censorship look like an aside, but it holds the word to be cut.
explanation.definitionFit: To react is to respond to something, so having offered a response is the past tense of that verb.

clue.text: Hold about: dull way of learning subject in food science

indicators.note: about here means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: to pin is to hold fast
learning by rote is repetitive memorising

explanation.surface: Someone complains that food science lessons are taught by tedious memorisation.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'Hold about' look like a pause before a gripe; it is the outer word placed around the learning method.
explanation.definitionFit: Proteins are one of the main nutrients studied in nutrition and food science, alongside fats and carbohydrates.

clue.text: Five gold cases aunt misappropriated somewhere in South Pacific

indicators.note: misappropriated money is wrongly diverted, so the letters are put in the wrong order
to case something is to enclose it, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
taken as written

explanation.surface: An aunt embezzled five gold cases while living on a Pacific island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases' reads as a plural noun counted by 'Five', but it is a verb: the gold goes round the scrambled relative.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an island nation in Melanesia, east of Australia, so it is one example of a place in the South Pacific.

clue.text: Before today, author Sinclair seen with pained expression

blocks.note: Upton Sinclair was the American author of The Jungle
an exclamation of pain

explanation.surface: A writer was previously photographed looking as if he were hurting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pained expression' suggests a face, but it is the word someone says when hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means until the present moment, which is the same span of time as everything prior to today.

clue.text: Qualifying match entered, reserve gets roasted again?

definitions.note: a past participle standing for a present-tense verb; the question mark admits the stretch

indicators.note: something that has entered is now inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: res is the abbreviation for reserve
a heat is a preliminary round deciding who goes through

explanation.surface: A substitute is sent into a qualifying race and is torn apart by the critics again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roasted' reads as harshly criticised, the sporting sense, but the answer is about warming food up a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: Warming food that has already been cooked once is giving it heat for a second time, loosely a repeat roasting.

clue.text: Ingredient of madeira is ... insidiously ... some old grapes

indicators.note: an ingredient is something contained in a mixture, so the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: letters running from the end of the first word across the second and into the third

explanation.surface: A wine buff notes that Madeira's flavour quietly includes a hint of aged fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipses are padding for the surface; the letters run straight across them.
explanation.definitionFit: Dried grapes become this fruit, so some grapes that have aged and shrivelled fit the definition well enough.

clue.text: After training, Perth girl is more nimble

indicators.note: training reshapes a body, so these letters are worked into another form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman from Perth has been working out and is now quicker on her feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a fitness report on an Australian or Scottish girl; every letter of the three words is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprightly means lively and quick in movement, so the comparative form is the equivalent of more agile.

clue.text: Fantastic, seeing a jewel mounted

indicators.note: in a down entry, mounting means climbing upward, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: a gem is a jewel

explanation.surface: Someone is thrilled to see a jewel set in its ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mounted' looks like the jeweller's sense of a stone set in a setting, but in a down clue it means the letters climb upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal slang adjective of praise, meaning excellent or great, interchangeable with words like brilliant or awesome.

clue.text: We're told to set kind of update

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: the sun sets as it sinks below the horizon

explanation.surface: Someone has been instructed to configure a software update.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To set' looks like the configuring of a device, which suits the update, but it is the verb for the sun going down.
explanation.definitionFit: Synchronising devices brings their data up to date with each other, so it is a type of update.

clue.text: Treats ... treats injury

blocks.note: first meaning: frozen desserts such as ice creams
second meaning: applies cold to a sprain or bruise

explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word switches from a noun to a verb; the ellipsis hides the change.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun names frozen desserts, and the verb means cooling a swelling with something frozen to reduce it.

clue.text: In Tianjin, Tim ate lychees with a certain warmth

indicators.note: something found in a phrase sits inside it, so the letters are within the following words

blocks.note: letters running from the end of the city across the name, the verb and into the fruit

explanation.surface: A man called Tim eats lychees affectionately in the Chinese city of Tianjin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it just places the scene in a city; it also signals letters lying inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in a close, personal and affectionate way shows a particular kind of warmth between people.

clue.text: Rod's called out in hellish water

indicators.note: calling out is speaking, so the word is judged by how it is said

blocks.note: rods are sticks, read as a plural

explanation.surface: A man called Rod is shouted at in the hot water of hell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod's' looks like a man's name with a possessive, but it is the plural of a word for a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology this river divides the world of the living from Hades, the underworld.

clue.text: Cash in kind of roll from S African politicians

blocks.note: a Swiss roll is a rolled sponge cake with jam
FR is an abbreviation for from
the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

explanation.surface: Money handed over in a bread roll by South African politicians suggests a bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cash in' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'Cash' is the definition and 'in' a link. A Swiss roll is a British cake of rolled sponge.
explanation.definitionFit: The currency of Switzerland is money, and cash is just money in notes or coins.
